item.title: OpenAI’s Dots are always-on AI agents for work
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 1.44
Meta’s Muse agent was born to shop , while Gemini’s Spark can help you book airline tickets or plan your weekly meals. But while Muse and Spark act like personal assistants, OpenAI’s new AI agents are designed to be, well, another “you” in the office. Dots, which OpenAI boss Sam Altman just unveiled at the company’s annual developers conference , are always-on AI assistants that — as with Muse — you can name, assign cute little avatars to, and chat with in the ChatGPT interface, via text, or even on the phone. But OpenAI is also positioning its Dots as your “delegates” and “extensions” in the office, where they can take on work duties you’ve assigned to them, as well as collaborate with colleagues (and their Dots) on Slack, Microsoft Teams, or in the new ChatGPT Spaces environment. OpenAI’s Dots are workplace agents you can collaborate with via ChatGPT Spaces, Microsoft Teams, or Slack (pictured). Ben Patterson/Foundry Powered by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI’s “most aligned model,” Altman promised), Dots require a $100-a-month ChatGPT Pro plan or better, and can take on complex work and coding tasks, performing them locally or in the cloud before eventually coming back to report the results. Each eligible ChatGPT account comes with one Dot included, and users will eventually be able to take charge of multiple Dots. During the presentation, Altman was careful to emphasize that Dots let you “stay in control” thanks to Astra’s “built-in protections and safeguards,” while users are free to set custom instructions and boundaries for the assistants. “So this allows you to trust your Dot with as much responsibility as you’re comfortable with,” Altman said. Of course, OpenAI’s Dots debut comes amid mounting anxiety over the rapid growth of AI , with the biggest AI players calling for government regulation and “pacing” of frontier model development, while more and more AI whistleblowers are warning that AI could, quite literally, kill us all with the next decade. Just yesterday, OpenAI released a statement apologizing for an incident where its models hacked into Australian government websites, while another statement detailed new guidelines to bolster AI safety. But OpenAI’s peppy, Apple-style keynote belied the gravity of the moment, with Altman trotting out one agentic AI announcement after another, including GPT-6.1 Sol, a new GPT model designed to deliver Astra-level performance at a fraction of the cost. Also new is a ChatGPT Pro 500 plan, which at $500 a month becomes the priciest of OpenAI’s consumer ChatGPT individual plans. Aside from expanded usage limits, the Pro 500 plan also includes an Ultrafast mode, which boasts eight times the speed of standard mode at a whopping six times the price. Another subscription change involves the $200-a-month Pro plan, which has been re-opened to new subscribers while having its usage allowance cut roughly in half “to reflect our increasingly efficient models,” according to OpenAI. Pro 200 users (who will get to keep their current usage rates “for a bit”) are, quite naturally, already howling in protest . Then there’s Codex Security Cloud, a cloud-based that’s continuously scanning for vulnerabilities while spinning up security fixes, and OpenAI Private Intelligence, which sounds like OpenAI’s version of Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. I plan on testing OpenAI’s Dots once I scrounge up the cash for upgrading my Dot-less ChatGPT Plus account, so stay tuned. Updated to add details about changes to OpenAI’s Pro 200 subscription plan.

item.title: Adios, Gems: Google’s new Gemini skills won’t be paywalled
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.93
One of the easiest ways to create your own, customized Gemini chatbot is about to be retired, but we just got a pair of encouraging updates about their replacements. We learned earlier this week that skills, a Gemini feature that was previously reserved for the Gemini Spark AI assistant, would step in for Gems , and that existing Gems would be converted to skills in the runup to the November sunset date. One of the big questions about skills, which are essentially custom instructions for Gemini that can be summoned within a prompt, was whether they’d be available to free as well as paid users. Previously, you could only use skills with the Spark agent, and Spark is reserved for paid Gemini AI users. But in an updated shared Wednesday, Google announced that Gemini skills will be available for any Gemini users over 18 with a personal Google account. Google added that skills will also be upgraded with missing features included in Gems, such as the ability to share skills with other users. You’ll also be able to add files from Google Drive as well as notebooks from Gemini Notebook. Existing Gems will be converted to skills automatically, Google confirmed, or you can do the conversion manually if you wish. Personal Gemini Gems will be retired starting in November, Google said, while Gems created by Google Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will stick around until March 2027. Gems for Workspace education accounts won’t go dark until June 2027. Unlike Gems, which are essentially self-contained, Gemini-powered chatbots with their own instructions and knowledge files, skills can be invoked within any Gemini chat session by typing “/,” and you can even call a skill within another skill, allowing for powerful AI workflows. News that Google is phasing out Gems in favor of Gemini skills comes about two weeks after word surfaced that OpenAI is nixing custom GPTs , which (like Gemini Gems) allow you to create customized ChatGPT chatbots. Custom GPTs will be replaced by ChatGPT plugins.

item.title: Switching to New Outlook? Here’s how to move your calendar and contacts
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
If you’re moving your data to the latest version of Microsoft Outlook , it’s important to know that your calendar and contacts may need to be handled separately from your email. Classic Outlook can export your data in a PST file, but New Outlook does not restore calendar and contact information in the same way. Instead, you need to first export your calendar as an ICS file and then your contacts as a CSV file, then you need to import those files to the new version. Restoring your calendar To restore the calendar, open New Outlook and click on Add Calendar underneath the monthly view. Next select Upload from File, then Browse. Find the ICS file and select Open. Under Select Calendar, pick the calendar you wish to restore. Once you’ve clicked Import, Outlook will add the stored data to your current calendar. Restoring your contacts Now your contacts. Save your contacts as a CSV file. In New Outlook, open Contacts on the sidebar. They will appear there under the People tab. Next, click Export Contact in the ribbon, then Export. Outlook will then compile the CSV file with your contact information and save it to your local Downloads folder. Now open Contacts and click on Import Contacts. Next click on Select Browse for a File and upload the CSV file. Finally, select Open and then Import in the next window.

Note that in this article we focus on local-software based solutions, although many also include a cloud component. For cloud-first backup, see our roundup of the best online backup services . Admittedly, the distinction between the two categories is blurring as they each expand their feature sets. How we test Our reviewers run each program through the various types of backups and restores it’s capable of — including those requiring boot media. This is largely to gauge reliability and hardware compatibility. We check speed, but such is highly reliant upon the connections and media involved. If we notice anything is particularly fast or slow, we’ll tell you about it, but creating a functional backup is paramount. To learn more details, see our article on how PCWorld tests backup software . Who curated this article Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. How to choose backup software If you recently purchased an external HDD or SSD from a major vendor such as Seagate or WD, check to see if there are backup utilities or a backup software license included. Whatever backup software you use, keep in mind the following key aspects of the best solutions: file backup for documents/photos, image backup for whole-PC rollback, boot media for dead-drive recovery, versioning for accidental overwrite protection, and know which are critical to your backup plan. File backup If you want to back up your essential data (operating systems and programs can be reinstalled, though it’s mildly time- and effort-consuming), a program that backs up only your important files is essential. Some programs even automatically select the appropriate files or folders. File backup can include operating system files if you wish but is still not suitable for disaster recovery. Image backup/imaging Images are byte-for-byte snapshots of your entire hard drive (normally not including empty sectors) or partitions, and can be used to restore the operating system, drivers, programs in one swift, fell swoop. Imaging also ensures that you don’t omit anything important as can happen with file backup. Recovery boot media Should your system crash completely, you need alternate means to boot your system and restore data using your backup software. Any backup program worth its salt should be able to create a bootable optical disc or USB thumb drive. Some will also create a restore partition on your hard drive, which can be used if the issue isn’t a failed drive. Note that we’ve run into multiple issues with Microsoft’s own Recovery Drive and System repair disc — don’t rely on those. Scheduling If you’re going to back up effectively, you need to do so on a regular basis. Any backup program you purchase should let you schedule backups and run them in the background. Some even will backup files as they change (real time) or at very short intervals (continuous) Versioning Versioning is simply retaining older version of files (or backups) rather than overwriting them during the backup/sync process. You can generally define how many versions to keep, but if you choose to cull older files, this is till not true backup which again, is an immutable copy of your data, drives, or system. Optical discs Every backup program supports hard drives, but as obsolete as they may seem, DVDs and Blu-Ray discs are great archive media. If you’re worried about optical media’s reliability, M-Disc claims its discs are reliable for a thousand years, backed up by Department of Defense testing. Online storage (cloud) support An offsite copy of your data is a hedge against physical disasters such as theft, flood, fire, and power surges. Online storage services are a great way to meet that need. Some backup software will let you back up to Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, Amazon S3 and compatible, etc. however Cloud Managers can serve as a workaround with backup programs that don’t. The downside to cloud storage is relatively slow performance. Keep a local backup for faster restores. Network access Backing up to other computers or NAS boxes on your network or in remote locations (say your parent’s or children’s house) is another way of safeguarding your data via a physically remote copy. If you use network storage, it can also be handy to back them up to you local system. FTP/SFTP can be used for offsite, while SMB (Windows and most OS’s) and AFP (Apple) are good for other PCs or NAS on your local network. Network support is not universal, and some backup programs allow you to back up to , but not from network shares. Just be careful in the way you expose your computers on the Internet. Real-time backup Real-time backup means that files are backed up whenever they change, usually upon creation or save. It’s handy for keeping an immediately available backup of rapidly changing data sets. For less volatile data sets, scheduled backups will do just fine. Continuous backup Continuous simply means backing up on a tight schedule, generally every few minutes, rather than in real time, daily, weekly, or monthly. Use continuous backup for rapidly changing data sets where transfer rates are too slow, or computing power too precious for real-time backup. Performance concerns Most backups proceed in the background or during dead time, so performance isn’t a huge issue in the consumer space. However, if you’re backing up multiple machines, backing up to multiple destinations, or dealing with very large data sets, speed will be a consideration. That said, backup speed is highly dependent upon the hardware and transport technology in use. Further reading: Check out PCWorld’s roundup of best external drives for recommendations on reliable storage options — an important component in a comprehensive backup strategy. FAQ 1. What is the best Windows backup software? The best Windows backup software is Easeus Todo Backup 2025 . It has everything PCWorld expects to see in a top product: A polished interface, intuitive functionality, a comprehensive approach to backing up data including imaging, file backup, sync, and disaster recovery. And most important, it’s reliable! Todo Backup also offers the option of a perpetual license or a subscription model, the latter of which can be augmented with affordable cloud storage. 2. What is the best free Windows backup software? It turns out that PCWorld’s favorite for-pay backup software, Easeus Todo Backup 2025 , also offers a surprisingly robust free version. It matches its paid counterpart in basics such as imaging, file backup, sync, and, most especially — disaster recovery. It also features the same eminently user-friendly interface. As with most backup freeware, you will be nagged to upgrade, and Easeus’s optional cloud storage, which is surprisingly affordable, is only available at the subscription tier. 3. Will backup software slow down my computer? Backup software typically runs in the background or during dead time, so given even moderately modern hardware, you shouldn’t notice any decrease in performance. Most programs let you throttle the backup process if you do notice a slowdown. 4. Does Windows Backup and Restore (Windows 7) save everything? Yes, by default, Backup and Restore (Windows 7) saves everything on your system disk (all the partitions, including hidden ones) in what’s known as an image file that would be suitable for disaster recovery if Windows Recovery Drive and Rescue disk were reliable. News bulletin — they aren’t. Hence, we only recommend this program for creating highly compatible VHD/VHDX images of your data drives and partitions which can be mounted as virtual drives and browsed using nothing but Windows Explorer. 5. What’s the difference between Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, etc. and backup software? Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are what’s known as cloud storage , or online storage. They create a local virtual drive that you can drag files to, and which is eventually synced to the cloud as time allows. They also provide a Web portal where you can manage your files remotely. However, by default these services sync changes in the data across all devices. True backups should be immutable snapshots that may be added to but not changed. Some services offer versioning (keeping older files, and adding new ones), which creates a close approximation to backup. Cloud backup services (distinct from those mentioned above) offer many, though not all, of the benefits of Windows backup software. This is generally done with local client software that offers just basic functions like file backup and sync. You can learn more about these in our roundup of best cloud backup services . 6. How often should backups be scheduled? Ideally, as often as your data changes. If you are working on an important project or have work that you absolutely cannot afford to lose, you should consider real time (as data changes) or continuous (very short intervals). Hourly, daily, or longer intervals will be fine for the average user. All file backups should be augmented by weekly or monthly system backups. 7. Can I back up files to and from my cloud storage? Until a few years ago, most Windows backup software was restricted to making local backups — i.e., to another drive, external or internal, connected to your system. There were of course services such as Mozy that had their own backup clients, but that’s covered in our online backup roundup. Here we’re talking just plain backup programs. The situation is improving rapidly, and many backup software vendors are adding online storage services as destinations for their backups. If your favorite backup program doesn’t support cloud storage directly, a cloud storage manager that integrates online storage services into File Explorer can make online backup possible with just about any backup app. 8. What’s the difference between full, differential, and incremental backup? A full backup is a backup of all your data, regardless of how new or old it is. A differential backup is all the data that’s changed since your last full backup. An incremental backup is all the data that’s changed since any your original full and/or the last differential/incremental backup. Differential and incremental backups require a initial full backup to be restored. Differential backups require more time to create than incremental backups, but are quicker to restore since you only need the latest iteration. Differential backups can grow to be quite large if you don’t perform full backups very often. Incremental backups take less time to produce and are smaller, but take longer to restore as all of them created since the last full backup must be restored in the order in which they were created. 9. What’s the difference between image backup, system backup, and file backup? An image is low-level backup of all the sectors (including “empty” sectors if you wish) contained by a disk or partition, regardless of their pertinence to your files. It’s basically fool-proof in terms of accidentally overlooking important data. A system backup is an disk image backup of all the partitions on your system drive. This includes several that are hidden, i.e., not enumerated as drive letters by the operating system. A system backup might also include other drives, but must contain the OS drive. A file backup is a high-level backup of data read via the operating system’s file system. Most often this is data, but may include all the files on a drive. 10. What should I back up? In truth, it’s only your essential personal data that must absolutely, positively, 100% be backed up. Once the family pictures or your work-in-progress are trashed with no backup, there’s no way back other than an expensive recovery service, and even that’s not guaranteed if the physical media is unreadable. On the other hand, a system backup is exceedingly handy for getting you back up to speed with minimal hassle. It returns your system to exactly where you were at the time of the backup: OS, program, updates, upgrades, settings, data are all back in a relative blink of the eye. But it’s not essential. While reinstalling operating systems, drivers, and programs, as well as adjusting settings require more effort, you can then recover your data if that’s all you backed up. See the first paragraph. item.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is here. This prompt stops it from wasting your usage
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The latest version of Claude Sonnet—Anthropic’s workhorse AI model—has just landed, and with it comes a prompt that could help keep any AI agent from leaping into action before making a plan first. Available now on the web, the Claude desktop app, and other Claude platforms, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is Anthropic’s middle-of-the-road model , It’s a step below Opus 5.5 but apparently just as capable as Fable 5.1 (Anthropic’s pricey frontier flagship) and a step above Haiku 5 (a fast but basic Claude model that’s due for a 5.5 upgrade). In Anthropic’s benchmarks, Sonnet 5.5 achieves scores rivaling Opus 5.5 in areas such as agentic coding and computer use, although the latest Opus model is still on top in terms of “complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgement,” Anthropic notes. Still, Sonnet 5.5 appears surprisingly powerful and affordable compared to Claude Opus, and it also has the distinction of being the default Claude model for free users. In any event, with a new Claude model comes a new prompting guide , and the guide for the latest Sonnet contains a gem that could come in handy for other AI models, particularly those capable of building things. The prompt concerns “open-ended” requests, including those that don’t strictly define boundaries for what the AI should and shouldn’t do. An example provided by Anthropic is “show me what you can do with this,” with “this” being anything from an Excel spreadsheet to a code snippet. Like ChatGPT and Gemini, Claude can spontaneously start building charts, reports, videos, and other “artifacts” on the fly depending on your request, and an open-ended request could spawn an artifact you didn’t explicitly ask for. Needless to say, those artifacts will eat into your Claude usage limits—not great when you didn’t want them to begin with. In my tests, Sonnet 5.5 was pretty good about keeping its replies text-only when I handed it an Excel spreadsheet of made-up operating costs and asked “show me what you can do with this,” but in at least one instance it did spin up a chart on its own. I’ve previously written about prompts designed to keep AI models from jumping the gun, including one that directs an AI to stay in “pencil-and-paper” mode . But in Claude Sonnet 5.5’s prompting guide, Anthropic shares a new prompt for dialing down preemptive building: When the user asks for ideas, options, or a plan, give them that and stop. Don’t start building or changing anything until they say to go ahead. You can use that prompt (or something similar) at the beginning of any AI chat, but it’ll be most effective as part of the AI’s custom instructions, or in the case of Claude Code as part of your CLAUDE.md file . Even if you don’t use this particular Anthropic prompt, it’s a good reminder to be specific when asking an AI assistant or coding agent to do something—or not to do something, as it were.

item.title: Discord’s age verification is less terrible than I expected
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Back in February, Discord first attempted to launch its age verification process—only to run straight into massive user outcry. In response, the company went back to the drawing board. Now, half a year later, the branding of teen and adult accounts has finally rolled out. As a regular Discord user, I wasn’t sure what to expect from the process. So, while waiting my turn, I read up on what I needed to know. You can’t opt out Discord first framed age verification on the platform as a move to protect teens. Problem was, it expected users to submit to a facial scan or upload a government ID. That sparked protest—and rightfully so, given today’s greater privacy and security concerns. Now Discord has easier methods to prove adulthood , if you somehow get flagged as a teen. But you can’t escape the classification process. Multiple countries have begun requiring companies to confirm the ages of users, in order to protect children from harmful content and exposure to unsafe adults. The only true way to opt out is to leave the platform all together. Verification is now less invasive If you stick around, Discord automatically assigns you an age group based on what it calls “signals.” Using machine learning, the platform guesses your age based on details like how old your account is, who you speak with the most, the servers you belong to, and if you’ve ever subscribed to Nitro. Discord says it does not read your messages (either those sent on servers or over direct message) as part of its evaluation. According to Discord, this method will accurately assign an age category to over 90 percent of users. If it doesn’t, adults can prove their age through credit card info, the Apple App Store or Google Play Store, Google Wallet, or AgeKey. ( AgeKey is a service owned by Singaporean age verification company k-ID.) Discord says its third-party vendors for age confirmation must abide by its data retention policies. Namely, any age verification related data can only be kept for the time needed to confirm age, then must be deleted after. If facial age estimation comes into play, it can only be performed on your device. You can choose not to verify Still don’t want Discord to have any further information about you in order to escape classification as a teen? You can still keep using the platform, but your access will be more locked down. Teen accounts are restricted from age-gated servers, content, and settings. Messages with sensitive content may be blurred or all together blocked, depending on the source. Direct messages from non-friends will automatically be sent to a message request inbox, allowing you to screen them before they appear in your normal DM list. (For the full details on Teen protections, you can read Discord’s full rundown .) Perhaps a small benefit: Discord is now enabling “spoiler channels,” which will let server owners sequester juicy info without having to age-lock them. (AKA the long-standing workaround.) Where to check your status PCWorld Head to Settings > Account . Under Account Status , you’ll see “Age Group.” Your status will be listed as either Teen or Adult . Anecdotally, users on PCWorld’s The Full Nerd Discord server have reported getting Adult status—and just before I filed this story, I received the same designation, too. So Discord may end up being right about its high estimates for accurately pinpointing “mature” behavior. (We’re all still emotionally unsure it was correct, though.)

item.title: Meta’s new VR headset forgot about the games
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
I have a medium-intensity interest in virtual reality gaming. I’m excited to try Valve’s new Steam Frame , and an older VR headset design helped me lose a ton of weight . VR, more than any other technology, has the potential to change how video games are experienced. So it’s a little concerning to me that Meta, the multi-trillion-dollar company that rebranded itself around a virtual reality future…doesn’t seem to care about VR gaming. There’s a lot of information to unpack here, a big complicated mess of stuff to use a highly technical term. But the core issue is that I think Meta, one of the only corporate forces actually driving VR gaming forward, isn’t. Welcome to the Boost Mode newsletter. Every week I share my insights on PC gaming, desktop setups, and hardware optimization. I also track down some of the most interesting PC and nerd news from around the web, plus a PC game pick you might not have seen elsewhere. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website ! How Facebook got to the party The discussion requires a bit of context. Oculus, the company that started the most recent push into VR, was founded in 2012. It released the Oculus Rift in 2013, a PC-based VR setup combining a headset, tracker, and controllers. The company was bought by Facebook in 2014, which eventually completely absorbed the former into sub-units. Various other headsets have been released, notably the Oculus Quest, based on Arm hardware and running a modified version of Android, in 2019. Facebook rebranded as Meta in 2021, essentially betting the farm on the “Metaverse,” a vision of the future of gaming, work, and the internet at large where everyone was operating in virtual reality and mixed reality. To make a complex situation pithily simple, it seems like Mark Zuckerberg watched Ready Player One , saw baby’s first cyberpunk corporate dystopia, and said “Yeah, I wanna be the bad guy from that movie .” The Quest series of headsets continued as a cheap-ish way for people to get into VR . At the same time in the middle of the pandemic, Meta-nee-Facebook tried desperately to convince everyone that wearing two pounds of tech on your face for eight hours a day, while paying the company for every interaction on the web, was a good idea. It, um, didn’t go well. Valve Running in parallel to Zuckerberg trying to turn the internet into his own digital fiefdom (in his defense, he’s has some success before!), VR gaming had a mini-renaissance. In addition to Oculus/Meta investing billions into VR gaming mostly focused on the standalone/mobile side of the equation, Valve was partnering with various companies to push VR gaming on the PC side. Notable releases include the HTC Vive in 2016 and Valve’s own-branded Index in 2019, both of which require a gaming PC. Valve picks up the torch The Steam Frame is the evolution of these products, operating as both a stand-alone Arm-powered headset, a la the Meta Quest, and a PC-connected headset like the Index that can play more powerful games. It’s very exciting for a lot of reasons. Valve recognizes the work that Meta has put into VR gaming, and it’s even trying to woo developers of the Android-based games that work on Meta Quest headsets onto Steam , developing games that play on the standalone Frame. Valve All good, right? Well, maybe not. We’re a little over a decade into what was supposed to be a revitalization of VR gaming. And while there are dedicated developers and players, including tons of fascinating niche hardware…the Steam Frame comes bundled with Half-Life: Alyx . A blockbuster, genre-defining VR game, which came out more than six years ago . The fact that Valve can’t be bothered to put together a showpiece title for its new gadget is less than promising, and not a great endorsement for a headset that costs $1300. Valve’s lukewarm debut for the new system isn’t shocking, all things considered. For all that it’s an absolute legend of PC gaming, Valve isn’t all that interested in making its own games anymore — it wants to sell the platform . That’s what SteamOS, the Steam Deck handheld, and the Steam Machine mini PC are all about. And with the PC hardware market essentially frozen thanks to “AI,” now is unfortunately the worst time to try to get people to spend money on a new platform and niche hardware. If anything, the Arm guts of the Steam Frame are more exciting than its VR aspect, because it means you might be able to play Steam games on much cheaper non-VR devices very soon. But if Valve seems like it’s gotten over a seven-year itch for VR gaming, then Meta seems like it’s ready to file divorce papers. Earlier this year the company cut over a thousand jobs in Reality Labs , the corporate descendant of Oculus. It’s cut funding to studios that were making VR games for the Quest series of headsets, which included Meta exclusives like Rock Band VR, Vader Immortal, and Resident Evil 4 VR . Meta Perhaps more concerning for anyone who went all-in on the “metaverse,” the company has kinda-sorta abandoned its Horizon Worlds product. This was supposed to be the anchor point of Zuckerberg’s virtual reality empire, the thing that he was trying to force his own employees to work on. At its height in 2023, the platform had less than half a million regular users — not exactly earth-shattering. Facebook-Meta is estimated to have lost the better part of a hundred billion dollars on VR and the metaverse push. When it announced the above cuts, its stock price rose . It’s now chasing AI, just like everyone else. Meta seems to think the future is now in a panopticon of pervert glasses , purposely created political misinformation , and simulated child abuse that fits within its terms of service , despite the platform apparently being afraid of the big, bad Virginia Woolf . And it’s not like the company is losing money — $186 billion in profit for the 2025 fiscal year — so maybe it’s right. The new headset That being said, it might seem strange that Meta debuted a new VR headset last week. The Meta VR Glasses are interesting from a hardware perspective, sort of a halfway point between Apple’s Vision Pro designs and more basic “VR” heads-up displays, like Xreal and Rayneo . They’re small and light, requiring no rear headband. They include eye tracking, like the previous Quest Pro. Meta And they don’t actually look like regular eyeglasses, despite being called “Meta VR Glasses.” So you’re more likely to be mistaken for an X-Men cosplayer than someone who’s memorized the laws of recording consent in your state or country. A real bonus! Perhaps most compelling in terms of actual use case, Meta has highlighted these glasses’ utility as an entertainment machine with high-quality pancake lenses and OLED screens, and their ability to actually do work, thanks to a built-in quasi-desktop environment. Combined with a shockingly low weight thanks to its puck design — the headset is seven times lighter than the Vision Pro! — it looks like a genuine leap forward in comfort and design, if not in total utility. Meta Hey look at that, I’m three paragraphs into talking about the Meta VR Glasses. It feels like I forgot to talk about something. Oh, that’s right. GAMES. Despite making the best-selling VR headset of the modern era, and arguably being the driving force behind VR gaming for over a decade, Meta’s trailer for the VR Glasses doesn’t mention games at all. Hardly shocking, since this is also the first VR headset the company has produced without the Quest name attached. In the portion of the Meta Connect presentation announcing the new system, you get a demo of Beat Saber . That’s it. The seven-year-old casual game was shown off with no controllers, because Meta is focusing on hand tracking only for this headset. Despite a $1300 price tag, there’s no indication of controllers included in the purchase. “VR gaming is alive and well on Meta VR Glasses,” said Meta’s CTO, after playing a 2019 title for less than 30 seconds . It comes with the same level of reassurance that an octogenarian senator is in “excellent health.” The presentation also leaned on Xbox Cloud streaming, in the same way Google mentioned GeForce Now for its Googlebooks , before proceeding on to talk about movies. Meta Soooo yeah. Meta VR Glasses are impressive on a technical level. But if Meta is actually excited about VR gaming, specifically new VR games, it isn’t demonstrating that excitement to me at all. Considering how much it’s been dialing back its commitment to virtual reality everywhere, instead leaning into wearables and “AI,” I’m shocked this headset even came out. Rolling silicon stones I’ve been thinking a lot about corporate inertia lately. The Steam Machine and Steam Frame, Nvidia’s new RTX-powered laptop chips , Google’s Googlebook laptops. All of these products are launching at an objectively terrible time for consumers . Price tags are higher than ever, while other factors like wars, stagnant wages, and inflation are leaving consumers with less and less disposable income, even in wealthy nations. Alaina Yee / Foundry And yet these products launch anyway, even when practical wisdom might suggest they should stave it off for a year or two. The reason why — at least one of the reasons, and the one I’m most interested in — is corporate inertia. These products take years to develop, sometimes the better part of a decade. Billions of dollars invested, millions of hours of work from international teams. Once you get past a certain point of development, even companies as huge as Nvidia, Google, and Meta have to launch, if only to avoid throwing all that money and effort away. I think the Meta VR Glasses might be another victim of that, not that I’m particularly broken-hearted for any scheduling chaos on Meta’s part. While it’s incorporating innovations developed from years of VR headsets, particularly the Quest Pro , it’s also obviously taking a lot of inspiration from the Apple Vision Pro. And its most highlighted feature, the low weight, is a particular selling point against the Apple design. The fact that it’s less than half the price probably doesn’t hurt either. Apple I’m sure there’s a group of people who can both stomach giving money to a historically horrible company, and are also excited for the entertainment and utility in the VR Glasses. But I’m also sure that’s a pretty small sliver of the consumer electronics market. Meta doesn’t seem to be interested in courting gamers at all anymore, either at the low end for the Quest headsets, or in the $1300 range that the Steam Frame is targeting. That’s a big problem if you’re excited about VR gaming. Even if you never intend to give a cent to Meta, the company’s platform and push for the Metaverse absolutely elevated VR far beyond where it would have been otherwise. However excited Valve is about VR, it simply doesn’t have the money or the muscle to push virtual reality gaming into the public eye like Meta can. Once again, let me point out that the Steam Frame is launching with a VR Valve game that’s six years old. If Meta can’t or won’t be that driving force, we might see this entire section of the market shrivel and die, put on the shelf for another decade or two. And that would be a real shame at a time when gamers are craving novelty and innovation like never before. Cool stuff from around the web PS5 games can be emulated on PC now : You’re going to need an absolute monster of a PC gaming desktop just to hit 30FPS, and only a few games work. but you can kinda-sorta-techically play all those PlayStation exclusives if you want . Somebody made a mini PC out of gold : It weighs almost 30 pounds and costs almost two million dollars . And because gold is a decent thermal conductor, it doesn’t need fans. But surely there was a better way to do this…like, you know, aluminum or copper. FanlessTech The Steam Deck makes a pretty good Mars rover controller : Not exactly shocking , since you can control a submarine with an old Logitech USB controller. Though hopefully this one doesn’t meet the same end. DLSS 5 mod working on AMD graphics cards : If you want the yass filter but you don’t have a four-figure graphics card from Team Green, now you have options. Microsoft drops Copilot+ branding program : Since Microsoft has helped make PCs unaffordable, it can’t scrape together enough RAM for some of its own consumer PCs to qualify for the label anymore. So goodbye, Copilot+ — too bad the keyboard button is sticking around. Game pick of the week: Art of Rally Funselektor Labs Racing games tend to get the latest and greatest in terms of tech, especially on the “sim” side of things. But you can enjoy racing without all the bells and whistles, even without any real element of stress. That’s what Art of Rally is all about: It’s a chill love letter to decades of rally racing history. With a sort-of-top-down viewpoint and a low-poly visual style, it almost looks like a mobile game. (I love the way the crowds of spectators can get onto the track, like in old rally racing videos, and I love even more that they’re little Game of Life peg people.) But there’s a deceptive amount of skill required to optimize these time trials, and you can get into a flow state easily. With the gorgeous, simple vehicles based on dozens of real-world classics, and tons of flavor text, the game loves to teach you about rally racing. Any you’ll love zooming through the countryside. Art of Rally is $25 on Steam , but can frequently be had for far less — it’s just $10 on Indiegala at the time of writing. That’s all for this week. Firefox 157 is out for Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android and the biggest change in this version is the new Nova design, which brings a more modern look to the browser. Mozilla has also fixed over 70 security vulnerabilities, and updates are also available for the Firefox ESR versions. The release of Firefox 158 is scheduled for October 13th, 2026. What’s new in Firefox 157? Now that Firefox has adopted a two-week release cycle, major new features are growing fewer and farther between. With Firefox 157, the focus is on the new Nova design, which has heavily rounded corners and subtle color gradients on surfaces. You’ll find 12 themes, each in light and dark variants. Mozilla has also brought back the popular Compact Mode, which groups elements together to save space—great for smaller screens. You can learn more about the Nova redesign and what it entails in this announcement post by the Mozilla team . Security fixes in Firefox 157 In the security advisory for Firefox 157 , Mozilla lists 76 vulnerabilities that have been fixed, 30 of which were discovered and reported by external security researchers. Mozilla classifies 38 vulnerabilities as high risk, 29 as medium risk, and nine as low risk. Among them, 32 are use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, some of which could be exploited to inject and execute code, and 15 of which could be exploited to escape the browser sandbox. Firefox ESR updates In addition to Firefox 157, Firefox ESR releases 153.4.0, 140.17.0, and 115.42.0 are also now available. However, the latter are only available for Windows 7 and 8.1 and macOS 10.12 to 10.14 until March 2027. In the ESR versions, Mozilla has fixed the aforementioned vulnerabilities that were also present in the code of these earlier browser generations. That amounts to 62 vulnerabilities in Firefox 153.4.0, 43 in Firefox 140.17, and 31 in Firefox 115.42. Firefox ESR 140 received its final update on September 29th. In two weeks, this version will finally be replaced by Firefox ESR 153. If you haven’t already done so, it’s time to start planning the switch.

Next to consumer laptops, its performance doesn’t impress, and new Panther Lake hardware threatens it at every turn. How we test laptops The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops . Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo , and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also deeply immersed in the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound. How to choose the best laptop What’s the best laptop style? Regular ones are fine for everyday stuff. 2-in-1s are cool because the screen flips around. Chromebooks are cheap and good if you mostly do web browsing. How much power? Depends on what you’re doing. For basic web or email, an Intel Core i3 or Ryzen 3 works fine. If you’re into video editing or creative stuff, an i7/i9 or Ryzen 7/9 is better. And if you’re handling heavy 4K editing or lots of apps, a Ryzen 9 is your best bet. Discrete graphics vs. integrated graphics? Gamers and video editors need a legit graphics card—Nvidia, AMD, something with real muscle. But if all you’re doing is YouTube, emails, and Netflix, the built-in graphics won’t hold you back. How much RAM? RAM is more important than ever , especially with AI-powered features using more memory. 16GB is the sweet spot for most folks today. 8GB is fine for the basic stuff, but can quickly feeling limiting after a year or so. 32GB or more is ideal for gaming, heavy multitasking, and content creation. What’s the right display size? Doing video edits? Go bigger—15 or 17 inches helps a ton. For everyday use, 13 or 14 inches usually does the trick. Light enough to toss in your bag, not a pain to carry, and still plenty of space to get stuff done. Battery-life expectations If you’re gonna carry your laptop around, try to get one that lasts 10 to 12 hours on a charge. That’s usually enough for a long flight or a full day of classes. Some of the new Snapdragon laptops are even crushing that, with one going up to 25 hours thanks to their super-efficient chips . Just remember, bigger batteries usually mean heavier laptops. Laptop pricing guide A decent laptop usually runs $500 to $750. If money’s tight, a Chromebook or a basic work laptop under $500 will get you by. Push closer to $1,000 and you’ll start seeing nicer screens and more speed, but it really depends on what you need. Don’t forget the ports I like laptops with lots of ports so you don’t need adapters. Having both USB-C and USB-A is great. An HDMI port is especially useful for hooking up to an external monitor, especially if your laptop display just isn’t cutting it the way you want it to. FAQ 1. What is the best laptop? PCWorld calls the Acer Swift 16 AI the best overall laptop. It delivers fast, responsive performance thanks to Intel’s Panther Lake platform, handles multitasking without breaking a sweat, and packs impressive battery life for a 16-inch OLED machine, lasting around 18.5 hours in testing. 2. What is the best cheap laptop? The MacBook Neo is PCWorld’s favorite budget pick. It packs Apple’s A19 Pro chip, which delivers plenty of speed for everyday work and browsing. You also get a gorgeous 13-inch Liquid Retina display and a premium aluminum design. 3. What is the best gaming laptop? The Alienware 16X Aurora is a powerful gaming laptop that handles modern games with ease and makes them look amazing. It’s got an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX CPU and RTX 5070 graphics, so performance is top-notch without going overboard on price. 4. When is the best time to buy a laptop? The best time to buy a laptop is usually during big sales events like Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Back-to-school season’s also good. 5. What is a 2-in-1 laptop? A 2-in-1 is a flexible laptop that can flip and fold, more or less–basically, the acrobat of the laptop world. Want to kick back and watch Netflix? Prop it up like a tent. Need to take notes at your next meeting? Fold the keyboard back and jot things down on the touchscreen. They’re a hit with students and creatives who want a bit of everything in one device. 6. What is a Copilot+ laptop? A Copilot+ laptop is a PC with AI built right in. It helps you draft emails, generate images, and more. Since the AI runs locally, AI performance should be snappier. But at the end of the day, it’s still just a normal laptop (more or less), with a little helper that makes life easier to manage. To qualify as a Copilot+ laptop, though, it needs an NPU that can meet 40 TOPS of performance. item.title: Windows 11 26H2 update has known issues. You might want to wait
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Windows 11 26H2 is here earlier than expected, but before you run off and install it, you might want to take a second. Microsoft has issued a warning that the update contains a few known issues. According to the Windows Release Health notes : USB audio devices might fail to start or produce no sound , meaning some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices display Code 10 or fail in multichannel audio modes after installing the September 2026 update . Domain-joined devices might lose their secure trust relationship with the domain , meaning some accounts protected by Credential Guard might be unable to sign in with valid domain credentials. Devices might experience a black screen or desktop loading issues after sign-in , which can occur in some virtual desktop environments. To be clear, these issues aren’t caused by Windows 11 26H2. In fact, Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 24H2 also show those same issues on their respective Windows Release Health pages. However, it’s possible for your PC to not be experiencing these issues now but start experiencing them once you upgrade to Windows 11 26H2. Meanwhile, if you’re already experiencing them, you’ll likely keep experiencing them post-update. While Microsoft has marked these issues as “mitigated,” the reality is that they still persist and Microsoft is still investigating solutions. What should you do? If you haven’t yet noticed the issues above and absolutely don’t want them to happen on your PC, you should wait until Microsoft reports that these issues have been fixed before installing Windows 11 26H2. (That’s our recommendation, not Microsoft’s.) It’s unclear how long it’ll be before those fixes are released—Microsoft hasn’t provided details. item.title: Ashampoo Backup Pro 27 review: Easy, effective PC backup, but not ‘pro’
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Friendly interface Drive, partition, and file/folder (plain and compressed) backup with versioning Support for network sources and destinations Supports some cloud storage services Cons No more true real-time or continuous backup No backup using the recovery media Our Verdict Backup Pro 27’s friendly interface helps new users through imaging, versioned file backup, and disaster recovery. However, some features that would render it truly “Pro” aren’t included. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $25 perpetual license I $16 per month subscription Best Prices Today: Ashampoo Backup Pro Retailer Price Ashampoo $25 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Despite the somewhat odd name, Ashampoo peddles some very effective software. Not the least of which is Backup Pro 27. For the average home user, it’s a friendly and solid backup solution. However, the program is still missing a couple of features that would make it truly “Pro” and ditched another — real-time/continuous backup — for version 27 . Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for comparison. What’s new in Ashampoo Backup Pro 27? Other than the aforementioned deprecation of real-time/continuous backup, Backup Pro 27’s biggest morph is a rather significant alteration to the workflow and the way it’s presented — i.e., there’s a new, friendlier look that can operate in both light and dark modes. Gone is the division between simple and comprehensive wizards. Now there is a single approach with all pertinent options packed into a couple of scrollable pages. It’s simple enough for anyone, and offers easy access to all the bells and whistles that advanced users might utilize. However, as mentioned above and shown below, missing in action this go-around is the “real-time” backup I tested last time. I used quotes because it was more continuous backup than real time, backing up at granular intervals (continuous), not as files changed (real time). Daily is as granular as scheduling for backups gets without tediously adding “New time entries.” However, even that continuous granularity is gone. While I found a way to back up hourly, or even every few minutes, defining it was exceedingly tedious — requiring a “New Time Entry” for every additional occurrence. Why? I suppose someone thinks that users never want to back up more than a couple times a day. Beyond that, the major functionality remains intact. Additionally, the program as a whole is more mature and stable. Indeed, I suffered none of the installation and operational bugs I did with version 26, which admittedly, was only a day old at the time I first tested it. What are Ashampoo Backup Pro 27’s features? Backup Pro 27 lets you image entire partitions and drives (incremental and full — no differential), back up files and folders with versioning (keeping older copies), and disaster recovery — including boot media. In case the term “imaging” is new to you, it’s copying all the data blocks on a drive into a container file. Generally, empty sectors are bypassed. Gone are the easy and wizard backups, but Backup Pro 27 steps you through creating both file/folder and drive (imaging) backups. Backup Pro 27 uses the relatively common .vmdk format as its backup container. This, however, is a feature that could be considered “pro” as it is the native virtual drive format for VMWare. The free VirtualBox also can open this virtual drive for browsing. However, browsing using VM software is only possible if you don’t encrypt the images (you can compress). If you do encrypt, you must use Backup Pro to mount the image and restore files. I think Microsoft’s VHD would have been a better choice, as you could mount those with nothing more than Windows itself. Just saying. Backup Pro must also be used for file/folder backups that are encrypted and/or compressed. File/folder backups that aren’t encrypted may, of course, be browsed using nothing but Windows Explorer. Backup Pro 27 offers a comprehensive restore function that includes bootable recovery media. While Backup Pro will create a rescue USB stick or CD/DVD, the usual option for creating an ISO image doesn’t exist. But what I also find less than “pro” is that the rescue disk is restore-only — i.e., there’s no facility for creating new backups when you boot using it. Many users will only want to restore, but backing up before attempting to solve someone’s software or hardware issues is something most pros do religiously. Backup Pro 27’s recovery environment. Note that this is a photo, I was unable to boot using this media into a virtual machine. Note that even if your subscription (see the pricing section below) expires, the rescue media will still restore backups. Backup Pro handily supports cloud destinations, including OneDrive, OneDrive for Business, Google Drive, Dropbox, Strato HiDrive, 1&1, MagentCLOUD, OwnCloud, nextCloud, as well as any WebDAV server. Some of those might be unfamiliar, which reflects Ashampoo’s European roots. Ashampoo Backup Pro 27 supports a number of cloud storage services , though not often cheaper S3 compatibles. Conspicuously missing from the cloud destinations are Amazon S3 and S3 compatibles, which often offer the best value. To utilize these with any backup software, use one of the utilities in our roundup of cloud managers . But this lack, again is not “pro.” One thing I’d like to see is Backup Pro show physical drives with their numbers and partitions grouped together in some fashion rather than separated as you’ll see below (the first two hidden partitions are on the same disk as Windows, but inexperienced users might not realize this. There is an info box saying pertinent hidden and system partitions will also be backed up when you select any partition on a bootable disk, the Windows drive in this case. A good thing, as disaster recovery requires all of them. Listing partitions on the same drive separately like this may confuse less experienced users. Back on the sunny side…. A couple of the very useful Backup Pro features are the ability to trigger backups on media insertion, and support for network locations as both sources and destinations. These do drift towards the “pro” side of the equation as many end-user targeted backup programs only back up to network locations. There’s also a handy “Check Disks” utility so you can determine the health and status of your local media. How does Ashampoo Backup Pro 27 perform? Unlike my first look at Backup Pro 26, version 27 performed flawlessly from the jump. Of course, this time I didn’t have the older version installed which is what caused issues last time. Backup Pro 27 never glitched during any of the multiple tasks I threw at it: Imaging and file backup, local and online, encrypted/compressed, unencrypted/uncompressed, plus restore of all. This is the kind of message we like to see from backup software. Speed-wise, all was about par for the course given the media used for the destination. When I say par, backup software generally operates at around half the maximum transfer rate of any given media. How much is Ashampoo Backup Pro 27? A perpetual license for Backup Pro 27 was available at the time of this writing for $25, discounted from $66. You can also rent it for $16 per year, though I’d stick with uncompressed, unencrypted backups if a subscription is your choice. Otherwise you’ll only be able to restore those compressed/encrypted backups from the recovery disc if and when the subscription lapses. Those discounted prices are lower than I saw last time when the perpetual version was $33 and the yearly was $18. Backup Pro has come down in price since my last look at version 26. Should you buy Ashampoo Backup Pro 27? Backup Pro 27’s support for so many common backup chores, plus its comprehensive, easy-to-understand interface are major selling points for less-experienced users. If it meets your needs (there’s a trial), at $25, heck yeah. But the lack of backup from the recovery disc, no differential backup, and the newly limited scheduling are definitely not “pro” in my book. I’d balk big time at the full $66 retail. I strongly advise that you don’t rent (pay yearly) Backup Pro as the program seems to be shedding features rather than gaining them. The pace of development in the backup space in general is so slow, not to mention largely unnecessary, consider that general advice. Unless there’s online storage involved, that is.
